A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Human3R and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices. The shared method and experiments can be matched reliably despite added sections and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original human reconstruction, global motion, camera pose, and depth evaluations, together with quantitative ablations and qualitative reconstructions.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds runtime measurements, controlled ablations, detection-resolution experiments, and qualitative robustness evaluations.

M1.justification: The frozen CUT3R/Multi-HMR architecture, human prompts, losses, tracking, and test-time adaptation remain unchanged. The new decoder-training and cross-attention variants are experimental controls. Additional cropping-supervision documentation does not establish a change to the proposed procedure.

E1.justification: The training dataset and named quantitative benchmarks remain unchanged. However, Section 4.4 and Appendices A.1–A.2 substantially extend evaluated conditions to crowds exceeding ten people, severe truncation and occlusion, partial-body captures, face-focused running/selfie videos, and extreme poses. This additional coverage is qualitative.

E2.justification: GVHMR and TRAM, already present in the global-motion benchmark, become comparators in the new mesh-projection and runtime evaluations (Figure 17 and Tables 5–7). The comparator sets in the retained benchmark experiments remain unchanged.

E3.justification: New evaluation designs include component-level timing across backbone configurations and datasets, mesh reprojection comparisons, cross-attention removal and decoder fine-tuning controls, and feature scaling from 1/8 to 8 with detection precision, recall, and F1 (Appendices A.3–A.4 and A.8–A.10). Existing benchmark protocols and Appendix C training settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial robustness and diagnostic evidence: truncation/occlusion and partial-view cases, projection comparisons, runtime breakdowns, cross-attention ablation and visualization, decoder-training ablation, and feature-resolution sensitivity. Earlier human-prior, intrinsic-robustness, and naive-combination analyses remain, including v1 Table 4 becoming v2 Table 8.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-training uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The added average per-frame runtimes do not introduce uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: Retained benchmark and human-prior ablation values are unchanged. New results include ViT-S runtime of 13.59–15.87 FPS across datasets, Bonn depth Abs Rel of 0.086 versus 0.428 for the full model versus decoder fine-tuning, and detection recall falling from 94.9 to 55.8 under 1/8 feature scaling. New Table 10 also assigns retained human-error values to metric headings inconsistently with Tables 1–2.

T1.justification: The reconstruction equations, optimal-transport tracking formulation, and test-time state updates are retained. No new proofs or theoretical results appear. Expanded descriptions of standard reconstruction and detection metrics are explanatory.

C1.justification: The central unified reconstruction and competitive-performance claims remain. The introduction now attributes 15 FPS specifically to the lightweight model on an RTX 4090 and describes larger backbones as offering higher fidelity, qualifying the earlier broad statement about real-time operation without compromising accuracy.

C2.justification: The retained head-visibility limitation gains detailed explanations involving cropping supervision, token collisions, and tracking recovery. New discussion identifies missing-body motion failures, hallucinated extremities, and extreme-pose limitations. Appendices A.8–A.10 also interpret cross-attention as supporting spatial alignment, decoder fine-tuning as causing forgetting, and coarse features as causing missed detections.

D1.justification: v2 discloses supervision of the nearest visible point when cropping removes the head, specifies timing hardware and dataset resolutions, and advertises models and interactive demos alongside code. Appendix C remains unchanged. Conversely, the earlier explicit 60-degree field-of-view assumption for the baseline without intrinsics is omitted.

R1.justification: Both versions retain the same 117 references and unchanged related-work sections. New appendix discussion locally extends positioning against GVHMR and TRAM through projection quality, multi-person support, and computational cost, and connects possible future occlusion handling to PromptHMR's region-based prompts.

P1.justification: Most existing prose is retained. Changes include targeted introduction and caption edits, a rewritten intrinsic-robustness explanation, reordered appendix analyses, and updated affiliations and conference headers. The scientific additions do not entail a wholesale rewrite of the existing narrative.

P2.justification: v2 adds a human-prior schematic, extensive crowd and failure-case panels, mesh-projection comparisons, attention visualizations, and runtime and ablation tables. Existing displays are retained and renumbered, while the appendix is substantially reorganized around the new visual evidence.

improvement.justification: The runtime breakdowns, component controls, and explicit failure cases improve support for the existing design and clarify its applicability. These benefits are tempered by the qualitative nature of the new stress tests and apparent PA-MPJPE/PVE and WA-MPJPE/W-MPJPE column reversals in Table 10 relative to retained Tables 1–2. Overall evidence and transparency improve, but the new ablation reporting needs correction.
